sections.text:
Eleven men stand on a hill and stare at the sky. Jesus has just been taken up, a cloud has hidden him, and two men in white ask why they are still looking up. Just before he went, he told them what comes next: “You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” Acts follows that outline.

It continues Luke's Gospel. At Pentecost the believers are filled with the Holy Spirit, a community forms in Jerusalem, and persecution scatters it. A turning point comes when non-Jews are welcomed without being required to keep the whole law. After that the story follows Paul on his journeys through what is now Turkey and Greece.

The book ends with Paul in Rome, under guard, living in his own rented house. He receives all who come to him, preaching God's Kingdom and teaching about the Lord Jesus Christ with all boldness, without hindrance.

Acts is by the same author as Luke and addressed to the same Theophilus. Parts are written as we, which suggests the writer traveled with Paul. It covers about thirty years, from around the year 30 to the early 60s.

Christians differ on how far Acts describes the early church and how far it sets a pattern. Pentecostal and charismatic churches expect the gifts of the Spirit seen here to continue in the same way; others think some belonged to the founding period. Baptism, the sharing of possessions and the way churches are led are debated on the same lines.

Luke writes again to Theophilus. His first book was about all that Jesus began to do and teach. For forty days after his suffering, Jesus appeared to the apostles with many proofs, speaking about God's Kingdom. He told them to wait in Jerusalem for the promise of the Father, since they will be baptized in the Holy Spirit.

They ask whether he is now restoring the kingdom to Israel. He says the times belong to the Father, and then: “You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” He is taken up, and a cloud hides him. Two men in white ask why they stand looking at the sky, and promise that he will come back in the same way.

The disciples go back to the upper room and pray together. Peter speaks about Judas, and they draw lots, and the lot falls on Matthias.

Acts is the second volume of Luke's work, and Luke 24 ends where Acts 1 begins. The chapter sets the whole book's plan in verse 8. Many scholars date Acts to the later first century. The death of Judas is told here and in Matthew 27, and the two accounts differ in details. Christians have long discussed how to fit them together. Drawing lots is an ancient way of seeking God's choice. Christians differ on whether Matthias was the right choice, since Paul later calls himself an apostle too.

On the day of Pentecost the believers are all together in one place. Suddenly there is a sound like a mighty wind, and tongues like fire rest on each of them. They are all “filled with the Holy Spirit” and begin to speak in other languages. Jews from many nations are in Jerusalem, and each hears them in his own language.

Peter stands with the eleven and says it is only the third hour of the day. What they see is what Joel spoke of, the Spirit poured out on all flesh. He speaks of Jesus of Nazareth, crucified, whom God raised up, and says that God has made him both Lord and Christ.

The people are cut to the heart and ask what to do. Peter says, “Repent and be baptized”. About three thousand are added that day. They hold to the apostles' teaching, fellowship, the breaking of bread and prayer, and share what they have.

Pentecost was a Jewish pilgrimage feast, which is why people from so many places are in Jerusalem. The list of nations in verses 9 to 11 shows how far Jewish communities had spread. Christians differ on what speaking in other languages means today. Some see a once-for-all sign of the church's birth, and others expect it to continue. Peter's words to the men of Israel are a message from one Jew to other Jews, and the words about crucifixion have been misused against Jews, which is wrong. Compare Joel 2 and Psalm 16.

Peter and John go up to the temple at the hour of prayer. At the gate called Beautiful sits a man lame from birth, carried there daily to ask for money. He looks at them, expecting a gift. Peter says, “I have no silver or gold, but what I have, that I give you”, and in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth tells him to get up and walk. He takes his hand and lifts him, and the man's feet and ankles are strong. He walks, leaps and praises God.

A crowd runs together in Solomon's porch, and Peter speaks. It is not their power or godliness, he says, but faith in Jesus' name. He speaks of Jesus, whom God raised, and says he knows they acted in ignorance, as did their rulers. He calls them to repent and turn, so that their sins may be blotted out and times of refreshing may come.

Acts 3 shows the early believers still going to the temple at the hours of prayer, as faithful Jews did. Peter's speech is addressed to fellow Jews in the temple, and it is full of the language of promise and blessing. Parts of it have been misused to blame Jews for the death of Jesus, and that is a serious misreading. Peter says in verse 17 that he knows they acted in ignorance. Compare Deuteronomy 18 and Genesis 12.

Peter and John spend the night in custody, and by morning the rulers, elders and scribes of Jerusalem are waiting. The question is blunt: by what power, or in what name, was a crippled man healed? Peter, filled with the Holy Spirit, does not soften his answer. It was done in the name of Jesus Christ of Nazareth, whom the rulers crucified and God raised.

The council sees the boldness of these unlearned men and recognizes that they had been with Jesus. With the healed man standing there, they can say nothing against it, so they settle on threats. Peter and John reply, “we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard.” Released, they pray with their friends, the place is shaken, and they speak with boldness. The chapter closes on a community that shares what it owns, and on Barnabas, who sells a field and lays the money at the apostles’ feet.

Luke, whom tradition links to this book, picks up the story of the healing at the temple told in Acts 3. Peter and John stand before the same circle of power that handled Jesus, and the text names Annas and Caiaphas among them. At stake is whether the apostles may speak in Jerusalem at all. Peter's picture of the rejected stone echoes Psalm 118, and the community's prayer quotes Psalm 2. The shared life here recalls Acts 2, and Acts 5 shows what happens when that generosity is faked.

Barnabas gave a field, and everyone saw it. Now Ananias and his wife Sapphira sell a possession, keep back part of the price, and lay the rest at the apostles’ feet as if it were the whole. Peter tells Ananias the land and the money were his to keep. His sin was lying to God. Ananias falls down and dies. Hours later Sapphira, not knowing, repeats the story and meets the same end. Great fear comes on the whole assembly.

Then the story widens. Signs fill Jerusalem, and the sick are carried into the streets. The jealous high priest jails the apostles, but an angel opens the doors at night. Before the council Peter says, “We must obey God rather than men.” Gamaliel urges caution, the apostles are beaten and released, and they leave rejoicing, “counted worthy to suffer dishonor for Jesus’ name.”

This chapter follows the generous sharing of Acts 4, and Peter's words make clear that giving was never required. The sin he names is deceit. Christians have long read the deaths as a warning about hypocrisy within the community, and many find the story hard to read. The text records it without further comment. Gamaliel appears again in Acts 22 as the teacher of Paul. Scholars discuss how his examples, Theudas and Judas of Galilee, fit with other ancient records.

The church in Jerusalem is growing, and growth brings strain. A complaint rises from the Hellenists against the Hebrews: their widows are being overlooked in the daily service. The twelve do not brush it aside. They gather the whole community and ask for seven men of good report, full of the Holy Spirit and of wisdom, so that they themselves can keep to prayer and the word. The whole multitude is pleased. Seven are chosen, the first name is Stephen, and hands are laid on them. The word of God increases.

Stephen, full of faith and power, does great wonders among the people. When men from several synagogues argue with him and cannot withstand his wisdom, they arrange false witnesses. Stephen is seized and brought to the council, where every eye fixes on him, and they “saw his face like it was the face of an angel.”

Luke shows the first internal dispute of the church and how it was settled by listening and sharing the load. Many scholars think the Hellenists were Greek-speaking Jewish believers and the Hebrews were those who spoke Aramaic or Hebrew, though the text does not define the terms. All seven chosen men have Greek names. Stephen now takes center stage, and the charges against him, about the temple and the law, set up his long speech in Acts 7.

Stephen stands before the council that has heard the charge of blasphemy, and the high priest asks, are these things so? Stephen answers with a story. He begins with Abraham, a wanderer promised a land and given no inheritance in it. He moves through Joseph, sold by his brothers and raised up by God in Egypt, and then to Moses, rejected by his own people before God sent him as a deliverer. Again and again the people push away the very ones God sends.

Then the story turns on his hearers. The Most High does not dwell in temples made with hands, Stephen says, and you always resist the Holy Spirit. They rush at him. Stephen, looking up, sees the glory of God and Jesus standing at God's right hand. As the stones fly he prays, “Lord Jesus, receive my spirit!” and then, “Lord, don’t hold this sin against them!” A young man named Saul guards the garments.

This is the longest speech in Acts, and it answers the charge in Acts 6 that Stephen spoke against the temple and the law. Stephen, himself a Jew, speaks inside Israel's own story and in the style of the prophets, who also rebuked their own people. His words have wrongly been used against Jews as a whole, but the text aims them at the leaders in the room. Readers have noticed that a few details in his retelling differ from the accounts in Genesis and Exodus, and Christians explain this in different ways.

Saul was consenting to Stephen's death, and a great persecution scatters the church across Judea and Samaria. Yet the scattered ones go about preaching the word. Philip goes down to Samaria, and there is great joy in the city. Simon, who had long amazed the people with sorcery, believes and is baptized. When Peter and John arrive, they pray, lay on hands, and the Spirit is given. Simon offers money for such power, and Peter rebukes him sharply and calls him to repent.

Then an angel sends Philip to a desert road, where an Ethiopian eunuch, an official under the queen, sits in his chariot reading Isaiah. Philip asks, “Do you understand what you are reading?” The man answers, “How can I, unless someone explains it to me?” Philip climbs up beside him and tells him about Jesus. They come to water, the man is baptized, and he goes on his way rejoicing.

The persecution after Stephen's death fulfills the pattern of Acts 1:8, where the witness moves from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and beyond. Luke now tells of two unlikely recipients: the Samaritans, and an Ethiopian official. The passage the eunuch reads is from Isaiah 53. Christians differ on why the Spirit came to the Samaritans only after Peter and John arrived, and the text itself does not explain it.

Saul is still breathing threats against the Lord's disciples when he sets out for Damascus with letters from the high priest. On the road a light from the sky shines around him, and he falls to the earth. A voice says, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” He asks who is speaking, and the answer is Jesus. Saul is led into Damascus blind, and for three days he neither eats nor drinks.

The Lord sends a disciple named Ananias, who is afraid of this man. But the Lord says Saul is his chosen vessel. Ananias goes, lays his hands on him, and calls him brother. Something like scales falls from Saul's eyes, and he is baptized. In Jerusalem the disciples fear him until Barnabas speaks for him. The chapter ends with Peter at Lydda and Joppa, where a paralyzed man stands up and Tabitha is raised.

This is the first of three accounts of Saul's turning in Acts. The others are in chapters 22 and 26, and Paul tells part of his own story in Galatians 1. Luke places it right after Stephen's death, with Saul at the head of the persecution. The chapter shows the church's fear and then its welcome. Barnabas, already seen in Acts 4, becomes the bridge between Saul and the Jerusalem believers. The Peter stories that close the chapter lead into Acts 10.

In Caesarea, a Roman centurion named Cornelius prays and gives generously to the needy. An angel tells him to send for a man named Simon Peter in Joppa. Peter, praying on a rooftop, falls into a trance. He sees a great sheet let down from heaven, full of every kind of animal, and a voice tells him to kill and eat. Peter refuses. He has never eaten anything unclean. The voice answers, “What God has cleansed, you must not call unclean.” It happens three times.

The Spirit tells him to go with the men at the gate. In Cornelius's house Peter says it is unlawful for a Jew to visit one of another nation, but God has shown him not to call any man unclean. Then he says that “God doesn’t show favoritism”. While he is still speaking, the Holy Spirit falls on everyone listening, and Peter has them baptized.

This is a turning point in Acts. Luke tells it carefully because it changes who the church thinks it is for. Peter, a Jewish follower of Jesus, enters the home of a Gentile and eats and stays with him. In verse 28 Peter himself ties the vision to people, not only to food. The story is told again in Acts 11 and referred to in Acts 15. Cornelius is described as one who feared God and was well spoken of by the Jewish nation.

Peter comes back to Jerusalem, and the news has gone ahead of him: Gentiles have received the word of God. Some believers confront him. You went in to uncircumcised men and ate with them! Peter does not argue. He tells it all in order: the sheet, the voice, the three men at the door, the Spirit falling on them as on the believers at the start. Then he asks, “who was I, that I could withstand God?” The room falls quiet and glorifies God.

Meanwhile, those scattered after Stephen carry the message farther, and in Antioch some begin speaking to Greeks about the Lord Jesus. A great number believe. The Jerusalem church sends Barnabas, who sees the grace of God and is glad. He goes to Tarsus to find Saul, and for a year the two teach there. “The disciples were first called Christians in Antioch.” When a prophet warns of famine, the believers send relief to Judea.

Luke retells Peter's vision from Acts 10 here on purpose. The repetition lets Peter's own voice settle a question that could have split the young church. After this, the center of the story begins to move toward Antioch, a large city outside Judea. Barnabas and Saul will be sent out from there in Acts 13. The word Christians is thought by many to have begun as an outsiders' label, but the text only says where the disciples were first called that.

King Herod begins to oppress the church. He kills James, the brother of John, with the sword, and when he sees that this pleases the people, he arrests Peter. But the assembly is praying, constantly, for Peter.

The night before his trial, Peter sleeps between two soldiers, chained. An angel strikes his side and says, “Stand up quickly!” The chains fall off, the iron gate opens by itself, and Peter finds himself alone in a street. At the house of Mary, mother of John Mark, the servant girl Rhoda knows his voice and is so glad she forgets to open the gate. They tell her, “You are crazy!” But Peter keeps knocking. Later, as a crowd cries, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!” an angel strikes him down, because he did not give God the glory. And the word of God grows and multiplies.

Persecution this time comes from a king, not from the council. The ruler here is usually identified as Herod Agrippa I. Luke sets James's death next to Peter's escape without explaining why one was spared, and the contrast has been felt by readers ever since. The praying house belongs to the mother of John Mark, who later travels with Barnabas and Paul. After this the focus shifts away from Peter, and Acts 13 turns to Antioch.

In the church at Antioch, while the prophets and teachers serve the Lord and fast, the Holy Spirit says, “Separate Barnabas and Saul for me”, for the work to which he has called them. On Cyprus the proconsul Sergius Paulus wants to hear the word of God, but a sorcerer named Elymas opposes them. Saul, now called Paul, declares that Elymas will be blind for a season, and he is. The proconsul believes.

At Antioch of Pisidia, invited to speak after the reading of the law and the prophets, Paul tells Israel's story from Egypt through David to Jesus, raised from the dead. The next Sabbath almost the whole city gathers, and some, filled with jealousy, contradict him. Paul and Barnabas say they now turn to the Gentiles, with the words, “I have set you as a light for the Gentiles”. A persecution drives them on to Iconium, and the disciples are filled with joy.

This opens the first journey of Paul and Barnabas, sent out by the church at Antioch. It is also where Luke starts calling Saul by the name Paul. The conflict in the synagogue is a dispute among Jews, and both Paul and Barnabas are themselves Jewish. The text has been misused against Jewish people as a whole, which it does not support. Christians read the words about those appointed to eternal life in verse 48 in different ways, some stressing God's choosing, others human response.

In Iconium a great number of Jews and Greeks believe, but the city divides, and when a plot to stone them surfaces, Paul and Barnabas flee to Lystra.

At Lystra a man who has never walked sits listening to Paul. Paul calls out, and the man leaps up and walks. The crowd cries out in their own language that the gods have come down. They name Barnabas Jupiter and Paul Mercury, and the priest of Jupiter brings oxen and garlands. Barnabas and Paul tear their clothes and rush in. “We also are men of the same nature as you,” they shout, and urge the people to turn to the living God. Soon men from Antioch and Iconium win the crowd over and stone Paul, dragging him out of the city. He rises and goes back in. The two strengthen the churches, saying that “through many afflictions we must enter into God’s Kingdom.”

This continues the first journey begun in Acts 13. Lystra is the one stop where the crowd is pagan rather than synagogue-going, so Paul speaks about the Creator and the world around them instead of quoting Israel's Scriptures, as he does again in Acts 17. The gods' names are Roman in the WEB. Paul later mentions his sufferings in 2 Corinthians 11. The elders appointed here show the churches being given lasting shape.

Some men come down from Judea to Antioch and teach that unless the Gentile believers are circumcised, they cannot be saved. Paul and Barnabas dispute it, and the church sends them to Jerusalem. After much discussion Peter reminds the apostles and elders that God gave the Gentiles the Holy Spirit just as he did to the Jews. “But we believe that we are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus, just as they are.”

James points to the words of the prophets and gives his judgment: do not trouble the Gentiles who turn to God, but ask them to keep away from idol pollution, sexual immorality, strangled meat and blood. A letter says that “it seemed good to the Holy Spirit, and to us” and is carried to Antioch, where the people rejoice. The ending is quieter. Paul and Barnabas disagree sharply over taking Mark, and they part ways.

This is often called the Jerusalem council, and it is the hinge of Acts. The question is whether non-Jews must become Jews to belong to the people of God. Paul gives his own account of a meeting in Jerusalem in Galatians 2, and scholars discuss how the two accounts relate. Christians differ on how the four requirements in the letter apply today. Some traditions have kept them, while many read them as guidance for that moment of shared meals between Jews and Gentiles.

Paul meets a young disciple named Timothy in Lystra, and he takes him along. Then the Spirit closes doors. At Troas Paul sees a man of Macedonia in a vision, begging, “Come over into Macedonia and help us.”

At Philippi a seller of purple named Lydia listens, the Lord opens her heart, and she and her household are baptized. When Paul frees a girl from a spirit, her masters drag Paul and Silas before the magistrates, who have them beaten and put in the inner prison. At midnight they are praying and singing hymns, and the prisoners are listening. An earthquake opens every door. The jailer, about to take his own life, hears Paul cry out that they are all there. Trembling, he asks, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” That night he and his household are baptized. In the morning Paul tells the magistrates they are Roman citizens, and the magistrates come to beg them out.

Here the story crosses into Europe, and at verse 10 the narrator slips into we, which tradition and many scholars take as a sign that Luke himself had joined the party. Philippi was a Roman colony, which explains the weight of Paul's citizenship later in the chapter. Paul's letter to the Philippians, written to the church founded here, is a natural companion. Lydia and the jailer are very different people, and Luke gives both a household turning to God.

In Thessalonica, Paul reasons for three Sabbaths from the Scriptures that the Christ had to suffer and rise. Some believe, but others set the city in an uproar and drag Jason before the rulers, shouting that these men turned the world upside down. Paul and Silas slip away to Beroea, where the people are “more noble than those in Thessalonica” and examine the Scriptures daily. Paul is soon sent on to Athens.

In Athens he walks a city full of idols. Philosophers bring him to the Areopagus and ask what this new teaching is. Paul begins with what he has seen: an altar to an unknown God. He tells of one God who made the world, who does not live in temples made by hands, and who is not far from any of us. He quotes their poets, then speaks of judgment and the resurrection. Some mock. Others say, “We want to hear you again concerning this.”

These three cities show three audiences: synagogue readers of the Scriptures, a mixed city crowd, and philosophers. In Athens Paul speaks about creation first, as he did in Acts 14, and quotes poets known to his hearers. Stoic and Epicurean philosophers appear in the text by name. The letters to the Thessalonians, written to the church begun here, are usually counted among Paul's earliest. Christians have found in the Areopagus speech both a model for speaking across cultures and a reminder that not everyone will agree.

Paul arrives in Corinth and finds a home with a couple, Aquila and Priscilla, who had been forced to leave Rome. He works with them at their trade of tent making and reasons in the synagogue each Sabbath. When opposition rises, he moves next door to the house of Justus, and Crispus, the synagogue ruler, believes with his whole household. One night the Lord says to him, “I have many people in this city.”

When the Jews bring him before the proconsul Gallio, Gallio refuses to judge questions about words and names and their own law, and drives them away. Paul later sails for Ephesus with Priscilla and Aquila. Then a gifted speaker named Apollos, from Alexandria, arrives. He knows the Scriptures and teaches about Jesus with fervor, but knows only the baptism of John. Priscilla and Aquila take him aside and explain the way of God more accurately.

Corinth was a busy port city, and Paul's two letters to the church here, 1 and 2 Corinthians, show how lively and difficult its community became. Claudius's order, mentioned in verse 2, and the name of Gallio are used by many scholars to date Paul's stay in Corinth to the early 50s. Priscilla is named before her husband in some verses, which readers often note as a sign of her standing. Acts 19 picks up the story at Ephesus.

At Ephesus, Paul meets about twelve disciples who have been baptized only into John's baptism and have not heard of the Holy Spirit. After they are baptized in the name of the Lord Jesus, the Spirit comes on them. Paul teaches for two years in the school of Tyrannus, so that all who live in Asia hear the word.

Some traveling exorcists try to use the name of Jesus without knowing him. The evil spirit answers, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know, but who are you?” and the men flee wounded.

Then trouble comes from another side. A silversmith named Demetrius makes shrines of Artemis, and he warns his fellow craftsmen that Paul is ruining their trade and the goddess's honor. The crowd fills the theater, shouting, “Great is Artemis of the Ephesians!” for about two hours, until the town clerk calms them and sends them home.

Ephesus was a major city whose temple of Artemis was known across Asia, and the text names the goddess and her trade. Paul's letter to the Ephesians and the message to Ephesus in Revelation 2 are linked to this city by tradition. Here the spiritual and the economic collide: Demetrius's worry is about money as much as faith. The town clerk's speech shows Roman order at work, and the Christians are cleared of charges of robbing temples.

On the first day of the week, in an upper room at Troas, Paul talks with the disciples until midnight. A young man named Eutychus, sitting in a window, sinks into a deep sleep as Paul keeps speaking, and falls from the third floor. He is taken up dead. Paul embraces him and says, “Don’t be troubled, for his life is in him.” By dawn the boy is brought in alive.

Hurrying toward Jerusalem, Paul calls the elders of Ephesus to meet him at Miletus. He says he goes to Jerusalem bound by the Spirit, knowing only that bonds and afflictions wait. He warns of wolves who will come, and he leaves them a saying of the Lord Jesus, “It is more blessed to give than to receive.” They weep, embrace him, and walk him to the ship, grieving most over his word that they will see his face no more.

The speech at Miletus is the only long speech in Acts that Paul gives to believers rather than outsiders, so it sounds a lot like his letters. It has often been compared with them. The narrator says we in much of the chapter, which tradition connects with Luke's presence. The elders are also called overseers and told to shepherd the flock. The saying of Jesus that Paul quotes is not found in the four Gospels, and the text simply says he said it.

The road to Jerusalem is lined with warnings. At Caesarea, the prophet Agabus takes Paul's belt, binds his own hands and feet, and says the owner of this belt will be bound in Jerusalem and handed to the Gentiles. He answers that he is ready not only to be bound, but to die for the name of the Lord Jesus. When he will not be persuaded, they say, “The Lord’s will be done.”

In Jerusalem the elders tell Paul that thousands of Jewish believers are zealous for the law, and that rumor says he teaches Jews to forsake Moses. They ask him to join four men in a vow. He does. But Jews from Asia see him in the temple, accuse him of bringing Greeks inside, and seize him. They are beating him when the Roman commander rushes in. As the crowd shouts, “Away with him!” Paul asks to speak.

Luke brings the long journey to its end at Jerusalem, and from here to the end of Acts Paul is a prisoner. The accusation about Trophimus, a Gentile from Ephesus, rests on an assumption, as verse 29 says. The elders' request tells us how divided opinion was about Paul among Jewish believers. Paul speaks about his purpose for this trip in Acts 20 and in his letter to the Romans. The commander, who thinks Paul might be an Egyptian rebel, takes him into the barracks.

Standing on the stairs of the barracks, chained, Paul speaks to a crowd that wants him dead. He chooses their own language, Hebrew, and they grow quiet. He tells them who he was: born in Tarsus, raised in Jerusalem at the feet of Gamaliel, zealous for God as they are, and a persecutor of the Way. Ananias, a devout man, restored his sight and told him he would be a witness to all people.

The crowd listens until Paul says the Lord sent him far away to the Gentiles. Then they shout, “Rid the earth of this fellow, for he isn’t fit to live!” The commander orders him examined by scourging. But as the straps go on, Paul quietly asks the centurion whether it is lawful to scourge a Roman who has not been found guilty. The commander is afraid when he learns Paul's status, and Paul adds, “I was born a Roman.”

This is Paul's own account of what Luke told in Acts 9, and he will tell it a third time in Acts 26. The versions differ in small details, such as whether the companions heard the sound or understood the voice, and Christians explain these differences in different ways. Roman citizenship protected a person from being beaten without a trial, which is why the commander backs off. Paul spoke Hebrew to win a hearing, but the mention of the Gentiles is what breaks it.

Paul, brought before the Jewish council, fixes his eyes on them and says he has lived before God in all good conscience. The high priest Ananias orders him struck on the mouth, and Paul snaps back, calling him a whitewashed wall. When bystanders object, Paul says he did not know the man was high priest. Then he notices that the council is split between Sadducees and Pharisees, and he cries out, “Concerning the hope and resurrection of the dead I am being judged!” The room erupts, and the commander has to pull Paul out by force.

That night the Lord stands by him and says he will testify in Rome also. The next morning more than forty men bind themselves under a curse to kill Paul. Paul's nephew hears of it and tells the commander, who sends Paul under heavy guard by night to the governor Felix in Caesarea, with a letter explaining the case.

Luke paints the council as divided between two groups that disagreed about resurrection, angels and spirits, and Paul uses that split. Christians read Paul's sharp reply to the high priest in different ways: as human heat, as prophetic judgment, or as something he regrets in verse 5. The commander's letter describes the rescue a little differently from how Acts 21 and 22 told it. The Lord's word in verse 11 sets the direction for the rest of the book.

Five days later the high priest Ananias arrives in Caesarea with elders and a speaker named Tertullus, to lay charges against Paul before the governor Felix. Tertullus begins with flattery, then calls Paul a plague and a ringleader of the Nazarenes. Paul answers calmly. It has been only twelve days since he went up to worship, no one found him arguing or stirring a crowd, and the real issue is the resurrection of the dead. He serves the God of his fathers according to the Way, with “a conscience void of offense toward God and men.”

Felix puts them off. Days later he and his wife Drusilla send for Paul, who speaks about righteousness, self-control and the judgment to come. Felix is terrified and says, “when it is convenient for me, I will summon you.” Two years pass, and when Festus succeeds him, Felix leaves Paul in bonds to gain favor with the Jews.

This chapter shows the slow grind of Roman justice. Felix, the governor, never decides the case, and Paul stays in custody in Caesarea. Paul's defense stays close to what he has said before: his hope is the same hope of resurrection that many of his accusers share. The account of Felix's mixed motives, fear, curiosity and a wish for a bribe, is told plainly. Acts 25 begins with Festus, the next governor.

A new governor, Festus, goes up to Jerusalem three days after arriving. The chief priests ask a favor: have Paul brought up to Jerusalem. The text tells us what they have in mind, an ambush on the road. Festus says no. Let them come down to Caesarea and make their charges there. They do, but they cannot prove them. Festus then asks Paul whether he will go up to Jerusalem to be judged, and Paul says, “I appeal to Caesar!” Festus confers and answers, “To Caesar you shall go.”

Some days later King Agrippa and Bernice arrive to greet the new governor. Festus lays out the case: the accusers had nothing criminal to charge, only questions about their own religion and about one Jesus, who was dead, whom Paul says is alive. Agrippa wants to hear Paul himself. The next day, with great pomp, Paul is brought in, and Festus admits he has nothing definite to write to the emperor.

Paul's appeal, the right of a Roman citizen to have his case heard by the emperor, changes the story's course. It sends him to Rome, as the Lord promised in Acts 23:11. Festus is trying to please the local leaders while following Roman procedure, which he explains in verse 16. His summary of the case in verses 18 to 19 is an outsider's view of the central issue: someone dead whom Paul says is alive. Agrippa is a Jewish ruler familiar with the customs, which sets up Acts 26.

Before King Agrippa, Paul stretches out his hand and begins. His whole life, he says, was lived as a strict Pharisee, and he now stands trial for the hope of the promise made to the fathers. Then he asks, “Why is it judged incredible with you if God does raise the dead?”

He tells how he once did all he could against the name of Jesus of Nazareth. On the way to Damascus at noon, a light brighter than the sun shone around him, and a voice spoke to him in Hebrew, appointing him a servant and witness. He was not disobedient to that vision. Festus interrupts, saying Paul is out of his mind, but Paul turns to the king. Agrippa asks, “With a little persuasion are you trying to make me a Christian?” Paul prays that all who hear him might be as he is, except for the chains.

This is the third telling of the Damascus road in Acts, and here Paul adds the line about kicking against the goads and puts the commission in Jesus's own words. The audience is Agrippa, who is expected to know the Scriptures. Christians have read Agrippa's reply in verse 28 as sincere, as ironic, or as a brush-off, and the text does not settle it. Everyone in the room agrees, in the end, that Paul has done nothing deserving death, but the appeal to Caesar is already made.

Paul sails for Italy as a prisoner in the care of a centurion named Julius, who treats him kindly. At Fair Havens Paul warns that the voyage will end in loss of ship, cargo and lives, but the centurion trusts the pilot and the owner. Then a violent wind seizes the ship. For many days neither sun nor stars appear, all hope is taken away.

Paul stands up among the starving men and tells them an angel has said, “Don’t be afraid, Paul. You must stand before Caesar.” God has granted him everyone who sails with him. On the fourteenth night the sailors sense land, and some try to slip away in the boat. Paul says they cannot be saved unless these stay in the ship, and the soldiers cut the boat loose. At dawn Paul takes bread, gives thanks, and eats. The ship breaks apart, but everyone reaches land.

This is the longest sea narrative in the New Testament, told by a narrator who says we. The Fast in verse 9 is usually taken to mean the Day of Atonement, which falls in autumn, when sailing was dangerous. The centurion, who first sides with the ship's owner, later saves Paul's life. Paul's calm here echoes the Lord's promise in Acts 23:11. Acts 28 begins on the island where they come ashore.

They have escaped the sea, and the island turns out to be Malta. The islanders show uncommon kindness. Paul gathers sticks, and a viper fastens on his hand. The people decide he must be a murderer whom Justice has not allowed to live. When nothing happens to him, they change their minds and say he is a god. Paul heals the father of Publius, and others are cured.

In Rome the brothers come out to meet him, and Paul thanks God and takes courage. Under guard, he calls the Jewish leaders together. He speaks from morning till evening about God's Kingdom,. Some believe, others do not. Paul quotes a word from Isaiah and says the salvation of God has been sent to the nations. The book ends with Paul two whole years in a rented house, receiving all who come, preaching the Kingdom “with all boldness, without hindrance.”

Luke ends Acts in Rome, the goal set out in Acts 1:8 and promised to Paul in Acts 23:11. The ending is open: the text does not say what happened at Paul's trial. The Isaiah passage in verses 26 and 27 is also quoted in the Gospels, and see Isaiah 6. It has been misused against Jewish people, but Paul himself is Jewish, some of his hearers believe, and he welcomes everyone who comes. Christians differ on whether the turn to the nations here means a final break or one more step in a story that continues.
